label: Landmarks You Can Feel (Lecture 17)
rows: ★ Sternal angle
The manubriosternal joint communicates with the SECOND rib: find the second rib for procedures, then palpate down and count.
★ Nipple line
Corresponds to the FIFTH intercostal space.
Fifth rib
Below the base of the fifth rib are the INFERIOR lobes; above it, the SUPERIOR lobes.
Jugular notch
Deep to it is the TRACHEA.
Larynx
C3 to C6 (the slide; the recording's "C9" does not exist). Cricothyroid ligament about 1 centimeter below the laryngeal prominence.
Neck triangles
POSTERIOR triangle: subclavian vein and lung apices. CAROTID triangle: bifurcation of the common carotid. The sternocleidomastoid divides anterior from posterior.

label: The Normal Chest Film
rows: First line
Chest radiographs are the most common radiologic study (radiographs = 75% of images ordered) and almost always FIRST for a pulmonary or cardiac complaint; pain and shortness of breath.
★ Posteroanterior vs anteroposterior
POSTEROANTERIOR = ambulatory, standing. ANTEROPOSTERIOR = supine, HEART MAGNIFIED: do not call it enlarged on that view alone.
★ Aortic knob
The rounded bulge at the top of the left mediastinal border (the aortic arch); pulmonary artery just below, then the left hilum.
★ Costophrenic angles
Sharp Vs where each hemidiaphragm meets the chest wall: "nice and sharp" is normal. Gastric bubble under the left hemidiaphragm.
★ Heart size
No more than HALF the posteroanterior span of the chest; one third right of the midline, two thirds left.
★ Hila
Bisect the chest; mostly pulmonary arteries and veins (plus fat, nodes, bronchial walls); LEFT slightly HIGHER; concave, similar size and density.
★ Trachea
Smooth radiopaque border, radiolucent inside, MIDLINE.
The rest of the read

Lungs radiolucent; retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces; only pulmonary arteries and veins as vascular markings; each rib one at a time, both sides; spinous processes midline. Lateral film: thoracic spine has a posterior arch.

label: Upper Airway Films
rows: Indications
Muffled voice; stridor (wheeze heard from the mouth without a stethoscope); suspected sinus infection; anterior neck pain.
Water's view
Maxillary and frontal sinuses, 45 degrees to the orbitomeatal line. For sinusitis: not really needed, but can confirm it and possibly REDUCE ANTIBIOTIC use.
★ Lateral soft-tissue neck
Trachea = the dark, patent, radiolucent air column. The esophagus sits in the RETROTRACHEAL space and shows NO air: collapsed = NORMAL when not eating.
Bones on the neck film
Slight ANTERIOR curve (cervical lordosis). The body below C7 is partly hidden by the FIRST RIB.
How to read it
Superior to inferior, left to right; airways dark; sinuses air-filled; bones continuous; always symmetry.

label: Is It the Film or the Patient?
rows: Good exposure
Vessels to at least the PERIPHERAL THIRD; paraspinous margins; left hemidiaphragm visible behind the heart.
Overexposed
DARK: thoracic spine, mediastinum, retrocardiac areas and nasogastric/endotracheal tubes show through.
Underexposed
WHITE: small vessels, NO spine and NO mediastinal anatomy.
Inspiration
Domes to the TENTH posterior rib standing (eighth to tenth seated or lying). Few ribs above the diaphragm = poor effort.
★ Rotation
Spinous processes to the clavicle borders. Do NOT use the tracheal shadow (a tube looks the same rotated).
The checklist

Trachea midline or deviated; lungs shadowing or lucency; vessels enlarged; HILA masses or lymphadenopathy; mediastinum width or mass; PLEURA effusion, thickening, calcification; BONES lesions or fractures; soft tissues: don't miss a mastectomy.

label: Choosing the Study
rows: Computed tomography first?
ONLY for a suspected pulmonary embolism: the computed tomography ANGIOGRAM. Everything else starts with the radiograph.
Radiograph indications
Chest pain, dyspnea, cough over 6 WEEKS unexplained, unexplained weight loss in any chronic SMOKER, hemoptysis, adventitious sounds, support hardware (lines, tubes, pacemaker).
Computed tomography

Most common reason: an INCONCLUSIVE radiograph with a continuing problem. Also embolism, trauma, chronic obstructive pulmonary and interstitial lung disease, BONE (rib and spine fractures), cancer screening. Head and neck: retropharyngeal abscess or foreign body the radiograph missed.
Contrast is for
VASCULAR pathology (embolism, dissection, aneurysm), focal lesions, the -itis conditions (magnetic resonance superior for vasculitis), METASTASES to lymph nodes.
Ultrasound
Almost exclusively TRAUMA: collapsed lung or fluid (extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma); procedures; NO contraindications. Ribs cast shadows.
★ Ventilation/perfusion

For pulmonary embolism when the angiogram can't be done (CONTRAST ALLERGY); INFERIOR to the angiogram. Ventilation: INHALED technetium-99m. Perfusion: INJECTED technetium-99m macroaggregated albumin. Result: low, medium or high probability.
Positron emission tomography
Higher resolution and sensitivity than single-photon, more cost; usually secondary to the radiograph; mostly for METASTASES; now done with computed tomography for a much CLEARER image.
Magnetic resonance

King of soft tissue, but the lungs' anatomy makes computed tomography first. Used for a mass INCONCLUSIVE on computed tomography, patients who can't have it, vasculopathy (second choice); SUPERIOR to the angiogram for INTRAMURAL HEMATOMA. Inflammation: dark T1, bright T2.
Who reads it
The radiologist gives the official read; the clinician's read is often just for the answer.

label: Contraindications and Cautions
rows: ★ Radiographs
NO true contraindications. Lifetime limit 100 millisieverts = about 10,000 chest radiographs or 25 chest computed tomography scans.
★ Pregnancy test

"Always, always, always": beta human chorionic gonadotropin (urine or blood) on every female of childbearing age. Pregnancy is NOT an absolute contraindication; emergent imaging is done, even with contrast.
Lead shielding
Everything not being filmed, especially thyroid, ovaries, testes, breasts, fetus.
★ Contrast cautions

Anaphylaxis to medicines; ★ SHELLFISH anaphylaxis not yet tested for iodine allergy; iodine anaphylaxis or angioedema; HIGH CREATININE or blood urea nitrogen (renally cleared, NEPHROTOXIC); suspected THYROID dysfunction.
Magnetic resonance precautions
Metal implants that are NOT titanium; gadolinium allergy (rare); claustrophobia.

label: Reading Computed Tomography
rows: Planes
TRANSVERSE (axial) = cross-section; FRONTAL (coronal) = both lungs, apex to base; SAGITTAL = one side in profile. A slice, not a stacked shadow.
Attenuation
HIGH (bright): bone (very high), FRESH blood, contrast. LOW (dark): air and gas, fluid, coagulated blood. NORMAL: heart and muscle.
Angiogram pearls

DESCENDING AORTA always on the LEFT of the patient's vertebral column; patient's left = YOUR right; RIGHT ventricle nearest the sternum; LEFT ventricle has the thickest wall; for an embolism the PULMONARY ARTERIES matter most.
Clot
A dark filling defect inside a bright, contrast-filled pulmonary artery.
Vasculogram
Almost always a computed tomography angiogram: embolism, pulmonary hypertension, vasculitis, scleroderma.

label: The Five Patterns
rows: Pneumonia
CONSOLIDATION (infiltrate): white, filled-in lung where it should be dark. Don't sort bacterial from viral on the film.
★ Pleural effusion
BLUNTED costophrenic angles; on computed tomography a gray collection compressing the lung.
★ Pulmonary edema
CEPHALIZATION of vessels, KERLEY B LINES (short horizontal lines at the outer lower lungs from thickened INTERLOBULAR SEPTA), pleural effusion, INCREASED cardiothoracic ratio.
Pneumothorax
JET BLACK air with the COMPRESSED lung beside it.
★ Interstitial lung disease

Diffuse abnormal patterns in the INTERSTITIUM, not the air sacs. Computed tomography: reticular (net-like), nodular (dots), HONEYCOMBING (cysts 3 to 10 millimeters), volume loss, traction bronchiectasis, GROUND-GLASS (hazy, pale), Kerley B lines.
